path: Group orders, element orders and spectra

results.title: Noncyclic groups of order 10 are dihedral
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite group of order $10$ that is not cyclic is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

results.title: Classification of groups of order 10
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite group of order $10$ is isomorphic either to the cyclic group $C_{10}$ of order $10$ or to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

results.title: Exclusive classification of groups of order 10
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group of order $10$. Then exactly one of the following holds: $G$ is isomorphic to the cyclic group $C_{10}$ of order $10$, or $G$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_5$ of order $10$.

results.title: Classification of groups of order 10, product form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C_n$ denote the cyclic group of order $n$ and let $D_5$ denote the dihedral group of order $10$. Every finite group of order $10$ is isomorphic to the direct product $C_5 \times C_2$ or to $D_5$.

results.title: Exclusive classification of groups of order 10, product form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group of order $10$, let $C_n$ denote the cyclic group of order $n$, and let $D_5$ denote the dihedral group of order $10$. Then exactly one of the following holds: $G$ is isomorphic to the direct product $C_5 \times C_2$, or $G$ is isomorphic to $D_5$.

results.title: The sum of consecutive squares equation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Integers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the sum of consecutive squares (SoCS) equation when $2\,b(b+1)(2b+1) = a(a+1)(2a+1) + c(c+1)(2c+1)$.

results.title: Solutions of the sum of consecutive squares problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A triple of integers $(a, b, c)$ is a SoCS solution when $0 < a + 1 < b < c$ and $(a, b, c)$ satisfies the sum of consecutive squares equation $2\,b(b+1)(2b+1) = a(a+1)(2a+1) + c(c+1)(2c+1)$, that is, $(a+1)^2 + \dots + b^2 = (b+1)^2 + \dots + c^2$.

results.title: $(2, 4, 5)$ solves the sum of consecutive squares problem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The triple $(2, 4, 5)$ is a solution of the sum of consecutive squares problem: $0 < 3 < 4 < 5$ and $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$.

reading_title.source: $(2, 4, 5)$ solves the sum of consecutive squares problem
parts: solves the sum of consecutive squares problem

results.title: Bounds on the ratio of the two spans
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every solution $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem, $1 < (b - a)/(c - b) < 1 + 2^{1/3} + 2^{2/3}$.

results.title: The Pell-type parameter is a positive nonsquare
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every solution $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem, the integer $A = 3(b - c)^2\bigl(12(b - a)^2(c - b)^2 - (a - 2b + c)^4\bigr)$ is positive and is not a perfect square.

results.title: Infinite families of solutions in a plane
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $(a, b, c)$ be a solution of the sum of consecutive squares problem. Then there are infinitely many distinct integer triples $(x, y, z)$ satisfying the sum of consecutive squares equation $2\,y(y+1)(2y+1) = x(x+1)(2x+1) + z(z+1)(2z+1)$, with no order or sign condition, such that $(b - c)x + (c - a)y + (a - b)z = 0$ and $z - x \equiv c - a \pmod 2$.

results.title: Solutions with odd span $c - a$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every odd integer $N \ge 3$ there is a solution $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem with $c - a = N$, together with infinitely many distinct solutions $(x, y, z)$ of that problem with $z - x$ odd, all lying in the plane $(b - c)x + (c - a)y + (a - b)z = 0$, which passes through $(a, b, c)$ and contains the line $x = y = z$.

reading_title.source: Solutions with odd span $c - a$

results.title: Infinitely many solutions with $c - a$ even
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are infinitely many solutions $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem with $c - a$ even.

reading_title.source: Infinitely many solutions with $c - a$ even

results.title: At most $2(N - 1)$ solutions with $c - a = N$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer $N > 1$, there are at most $2(N - 1)$ solutions $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem with $c - a = N$.

reading_title.source: At most $2(N - 1)$ solutions with $c - a = N$

results.title: No finitely many planes contain all solutions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a finite set of affine planes $ux + vy + wz = t$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with $u, v, w, t$ real and $(u, v, w) \ne (0, 0, 0)$. Then some solution $(a, b, c)$ of the sum of consecutive squares problem lies on none of the planes in $S$, that is, $ua + vb + wc \ne t$ for every plane in $S$.

results.title: Jacobi's identity for the cube of Euler's product
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$, the series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^n (2n+1) q^{n(n+1)/2}$ converges unconditionally to $(q;q)_\infty^3$, the cube of the infinite q-Pochhammer symbol $(q;q)_\infty = \prod_{n=0}^{\infty} (1 - q^{n+1})$.

results.title: Dehn group
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The Dehn group is the tensor product $\mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z})$ of abelian groups; it is the target of the Dehn invariant.

results.title: Edge of a polyhedron
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An edge, as recorded for the Dehn invariant, is a pair of real numbers: its length and its dihedral angle in radians. No positivity or range condition is imposed on either.

results.title: Dehn invariant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Dehn invariant of a list of edges is the sum, over the edges, of $\ell \otimes \theta$ in the Dehn group, where $\ell$ is the length of the edge and $\theta$ its dihedral angle taken modulo $2\pi$.

results.title: Dihedral angle of the regular tetrahedron
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The real number $\arccos(1/3)$, the dihedral angle of a regular tetrahedron in radians.

results.title: Edge list of a cube
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $\ell$, the edge list of a cube of side $\ell$ consists of $12$ edges, each of length $\ell$ with dihedral angle $\pi / 2$.

results.title: Edge list of the regular tetrahedron
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $\ell$, the edge list of a regular tetrahedron with edge length $\ell$ is the list of $6$ edges, each of length $\ell$ and dihedral angle $\arccos(1/3)$.

results.title: Dehn invariant of the empty edge list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The empty list of edges has Dehn invariant $0$.

results.title: The Dehn invariant splits off the first edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be an edge of length $\ell$ and dihedral angle $\theta$, and let $L$ be a list of edges. Then the Dehn invariant of the list obtained by putting $e$ in front of $L$ equals $\ell \otimes \theta$ plus the Dehn invariant of $L$, where $\theta$ is taken modulo $2\pi$.

results.title: Additivity of the Dehn invariant under concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists of edges $L_1$ and $L_2$, the Dehn invariant of the concatenation of $L_1$ and $L_2$ is the sum of the Dehn invariants of $L_1$ and $L_2$.

results.title: Dehn invariant of a repeated edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $n$ and an edge of length $\ell$ and dihedral angle $\theta$, the Dehn invariant of the list consisting of $n$ copies of that edge is $n \cdot (\ell \otimes \theta)$ in the Dehn group, where $\theta$ is taken modulo $2\pi$.

results.title: A $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional separating $\alpha$ from $\pi$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a real number such that $\alpha / \pi$ is irrational. Then there is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(\pi) = 0$ and $f(\alpha) \neq 0$.

reading_title.source: A $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional separating $\alpha$ from $\pi$

results.title: Nonvanishing of an edge term in the Dehn group
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\ell$ and $\alpha$ be real numbers with $\ell \neq 0$ and $\alpha / \pi$ irrational. Then the pure tensor $\ell \otimes [\alpha]$ is nonzero in the Dehn group $\mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R} / 2\pi\mathbb{Z})$, where $[\alpha]$ is the class of $\alpha$ modulo $2\pi$.

results.title: The Dehn invariant of the cube is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real number $\ell$, the edge list of a cube of side $\ell$ (twelve edges of length $\ell$, each with dihedral angle $\pi / 2$) has Dehn invariant $0$.

results.title: Nonzero Dehn invariant of the regular tetrahedron, conditional on irrationality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose that $\arccos(1/3) / \pi$ is irrational. Then for every nonzero real number $\ell$, the edge list of a regular tetrahedron of side $\ell$ (six edges of length $\ell$, each with dihedral angle $\arccos(1/3)$) has nonzero Dehn invariant.

results.title: Conditionally, the cube and the regular tetrahedron have different Dehn invariants
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose that $\arccos(1/3) / \pi$ is irrational. Then for all real numbers $\ell$ and $\ell'$ with $\ell' \ne 0$, the edge list of a cube of side $\ell$ and the edge list of a regular tetrahedron of side $\ell'$ have different Dehn invariants.

results.title: Negative binomial mass function with real shape
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Negative binomial mass `P(X = k) = r^{(k)} / k! · p ^ r · (1 - p) ^ k` with real shape `r` (rising factorial `r^{(k)} = (ascPochhammer ℝ k).eval r`) and success probability `p`, using the real power `p ^ r`. A probability mass function for `r > 0` and `p ∈ (0, 1]`.

results.title: Beta-binomial mass function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Beta-binomial mass `C(n, k) α^{(k)} β^{(n - k)} / (α + β)^{(n)}` (zero for `k > n`, since `C(n, k) = 0`). A probability mass function for `α, β > 0`.

results.title: Chu–Vandermonde identity for rising factorials
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `(α + β)^{(n)} = ∑_{k ≤ n} C(n, k) α^{(k)} β^{(n - k)}`, for all real `α, β`.

results.title: Beta-binomial masses sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The beta-binomial masses sum to one for `α, β > 0`.

results.title: Negative binomial masses sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The negative binomial masses sum to one for `r > 0` and `p ∈ (0, 1]` (the binomial series `∑ₖ r^{(k)} xᵏ / k! = (1 - x)^{-r}` at `x = 1 - p`).

results.title: Convolution of negative binomial laws with a common `p`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `∑_{k ≤ n} NB(r₁, p)(k) NB(r₂, p)(n - k) = NB(r₁ + r₂, p)(n)` for `p > 0` and all real shapes.

results.title: Negative binomial splitting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `r₁, r₂ > 0`, `0 < p < 1` and `k ≤ n`, `NB(r₁, p)(k) NB(r₂, p)(n - k) / NB(r₁ + r₂, p)(n) = BB(n; r₁, r₂)(k)`; the conditional law of one component given the total is beta-binomial and does not depend on `p`.

results.title: Negative binomial splitting for random variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `X` and `Y` are independent with `P(X = j) = NB(r₁, p)(j)` and `P(Y = j) = NB(r₂, p)(j)` for all `j`, where `r₁, r₂ > 0` and `0 < p < 1`, then `P(X = k ∣ X + Y = n) = BB(n; r₁, r₂)(k)` for `k ≤ n`.

results.title: Mean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `α, β > 0`, `E M = n α / (α + β) = n π`.

results.title: Second factorial moment
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Variance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Variance (Dolzhenko–Smith parametrization). For `α, β > 0`, with `π = α / (α + β)` and `γ = 1 / (α + β + 1)`, `Var M = E M² - (E M)² = n π (1 - π) (1 + (n - 1) γ)`.

results.title: Mixed Poisson mass function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mixed Poisson mass function `p(k) = ∫ e^{-λ} λ^k / k! dν(λ)` for a mixing law `ν` of the rate. It is a probability mass function when `ν` is a probability measure concentrated on `[0, ∞)`, which the theorems below assume; for such `ν` the integrand lies in `[0, 1]`, so the integral is never a junk value.

results.title: Zero class of a mixed Poisson law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The zero class of a mixed Poisson law is `E e^{-Λ}`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the mixed Poisson mass function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The mixed Poisson mass function is nonnegative when `ν` is concentrated on `[0, ∞)`.

results.title: Poisson mixture over a point mass is Poisson
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Poisson mixture over a point mass `δ_m` is the Poisson law with mean `m`.

results.title: Normalization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a probability measure `ν` concentrated on `[0, ∞)`, the mixed Poisson masses sum to one.

results.title: Zero inflation by mixing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Zero inflation by mixing (Jensen's inequality for `λ ↦ e^{-λ}`). For a probability measure `ν` with integrable rate, `P(N = 0) = E e^{-Λ} ≥ e^{-E Λ}`, the zero class of the Poisson law with the same mean.

results.title: Mean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a mixing measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with integrable rate, `E N = E Λ` (finiteness of `ν` is not needed for this identity).

results.title: Second factorial moment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a mixing measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable rate, `E[N (N - 1)] = E Λ²` (finiteness of `ν` is not needed for this identity).

results.title: Second moment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a finite mixing measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable rate, `E N² = E Λ² + E Λ`.

results.title: Variance decomposition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a probability measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable rate, `Var N = E N² - (E N)² = E Λ + Var Λ`: Poisson noise plus the variance of the rate.

results.title: Squared coefficient of variation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Squared coefficient of variation (Brennecke et al. 2013; Svensson 2020). For a probability measure `ν` on `[0, ∞)` with square-integrable rate and `E Λ > 0`, `CV²(N) = Var N / (E N)² = 1 / E Λ + Var Λ / (E Λ)² = 1 / E Λ + CV²(Λ)`.

results.title: Negative binomial mass function with size and mean
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The negative binomial mass function with size `θ` and mean `μ`: `NB(k; θ, μ) = θ⁽ᵏ⁾ / k! · (θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ · (μ / (θ + μ)) ^ k`, with the rising factorial `θ⁽ᵏ⁾ = Γ(θ + k) / Γ(θ)` and a real power `(θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ`. The parameter domain is `θ > 0`, `μ ≥ 0`; at `μ = 0` it is the point mass at `0`. Outside the domain the formula is not a probability mass function.

results.title: Mean parametrization is the canonical `p`-parametrization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0`, `negBinomialReal θ μ` is `negBinomialPMF θ p` at `p = θ / (θ + μ)`, since `1 - p = μ / (θ + μ)`. The two APIs are the same law; reuse the splitting and conditioning results proved for `negBinomialPMF` through this equivalence.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the negative binomial mass function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The negative binomial mass function is nonnegative on the parameter domain.

results.title: Zero class of the negative binomial law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The zero class of the negative binomial law is `(θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ`.

results.title: Negative binomial law with mean zero is a point mass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With mean `0` the negative binomial law is the point mass at `0`.

results.title: Zero class versus the Poisson law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0`, `P(0) = (θ / (θ + μ)) ^ θ ≥ e^{-μ}`: a negative binomial law puts at least as much mass at zero as the Poisson law with the same mean.

results.title: Greenwood–Yule
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Poisson mixture over a Gamma rate of shape `a > 0` and rate `b > 0` is negative binomial with size `a` and mean `a / b`.

results.title: Greenwood–Yule, mean form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ, μ > 0`, the Poisson mixture over `Gamma(θ, θ / μ)` (mean `μ`, variance `μ² / θ`) is `NB(θ, μ)`.

results.title: Normalization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0` the negative binomial masses sum to one. For `μ > 0` this is `hasSum_negBinomialPMF` transported along `negBinomialReal_eq_negBinomialPMF`, so the mean parametrization shares the canonical law's normalization instead of re-proving it.

results.title: Mean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0` the negative binomial law has mean `μ`.

results.title: Second moment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0`, `E N² = μ + μ² / θ + μ²`.

results.title: Variance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `θ > 0` and `μ ≥ 0` the negative binomial law has variance `μ + μ² / θ`.

results.title: Gamma–Poisson conjugacy, posterior
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With prior `Λ ~ Gamma(a, b)` (`a, b > 0`) and one observation `N = k` from `Po(Λ)`, the posterior density (likelihood times prior over the marginal `NB(k; a, a / b)`) is the `Gamma(a + k, b + 1)` density.

results.title: Gamma–Poisson conjugacy, posterior predictive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With prior `Λ ~ Gamma(a, b)` (`a, b > 0`) and counts `N, N'` that are independent `Po(Λ)` given `Λ`, `P(N' = j | N = k) = P(N = k, N' = j) / P(N = k) = NB(j; a + k, (a + k) / (b + 1))`.

results.title: Net probability flow of the immigration–death chain
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The net probability flow into state `n` of the immigration–death chain on `ℕ`, in which molecules are made at rate `κ` (`n → n + 1`) and each decays at rate `γ` (`n → n - 1` at rate `γ n`): `(κ p(n - 1) + γ (n + 1) p(n + 1)) - (κ + γ n) p(n)`, with no inflow from below at `n = 0`. A law `p` is stationary (global balance) iff this flow vanishes for every `n`.

results.title: Immigration–death stationary law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `γ ≠ 0` the Poisson law with mean `κ / γ` satisfies global balance for the immigration–death chain. The identity holds for all real `κ`; the chain is meaningful for `κ ≥ 0`, `γ > 0`.

results.title: Fano factor of the Poisson law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For mean `m > 0`, `Var N / E N = 1`; in particular the stationary law of the immigration–death chain has Fano factor `1`.

results.title: Bursty expression stationary law

results.title: Lattice cells
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a lattice cell in dimension $d$ is a point of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, that is, a function assigning an integer to each of the $d$ coordinate axes.

results.title: Face adjacency of lattice cells
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two lattice cells $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ are face adjacent when there is an axis $k$ such that $x_j = y_j$ for every axis $j \ne k$ and $|x_k - y_k| = 1$.

results.title: Polycube
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is a polycube when it is nonempty and any two cells $x, y \in S$ are joined by a finite sequence of cells of $S$, starting at $x$ and ending at $y$, in which consecutive cells are face adjacent.

results.title: Canonical position of a cell set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is in canonical position when, for every axis $k$, every cell $x \in S$ has $x_k \ge 0$ and some cell $x \in S$ has $x_k = 0$; that is, the minimum of each coordinate over $S$ is $0$.

results.title: Proper dimension
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proper dimension of a finite set $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the number of axes $k$ on which $S$ varies, that is, for which there are cells $x, y \in S$ with $x_k \ne y_k$.

results.title: Fixed polycubes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, the fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $d$ are represented by the finite sets $S$ of lattice cells in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that are polycubes (nonempty and connected through face adjacency), have exactly $n$ cells, and are in canonical position (the minimum of each coordinate over $S$ is $0$).

results.title: Number of fixed polycubes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $n$, $A_d(n)$ is the number of fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $d$, that is, the number of $n$-cell polycubes in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that are in canonical position.

results.title: Proper fixed polycubes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, the fixed $n$-cell polycubes proper in dimension $i$ are the fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $i$ whose proper dimension is $i$, that is, which vary along each of the $i$ axes.

results.title: Number of proper fixed polycubes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $i$, $\mathrm{DX}(n,i)$ is the number of fixed $n$-cell polycubes proper in dimension $i$, that is, of fixed $n$-cell polycubes in dimension $i$ whose proper dimension is $i$.

results.title: Lunnon's dimension decomposition for fixed polycubes
results.caption: Theorem

api: Extracting the minimum of a binary min-heap
Heap order on a level-order array
Binary heap extraction splits off the minimum

results.title: Parent index in a level-order binary tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the parent index of a natural number $i$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$, where $i - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so the root index $0$ is sent to $0$.

results.title: Left child index in a level-order binary tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the left child of the node at index $i$ has index $2i + 1$.

results.title: Right child index in an array-backed binary tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In the level-order layout of a binary tree in an array indexed from $0$, the right child of the node at index $i$ is at index $2i + 2$.

results.title: The parent of a valid nonroot index is valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an array $a$ of length $|a|$ and an index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ of $i$ is also less than $|a|$.

results.title: Heap order on a level-order array
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An array $a$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, is heap ordered when every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, where $|a|$ is the length of $a$, we have $a_{\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor} \le a_i$.

results.title: Arrays ready for sift-up
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, and for $j > 0$ let $p(j) = \lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-up at an index $i$ when $i < |a|$, when $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every $j \ne i$ with $0 < j < |a|$, and when, if $i > 0$, also $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) = i$.

results.title: Sift-down precondition
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For an array $a$ over a type ordered by $\le$, write $p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/2 \rfloor$ for the parent of index $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-down at index $i$ when $i$ is a valid index of $a$; $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) \ne i$; and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) = i$.

results.title: Smaller child
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and let $i$ be an index with children $\ell = 2i + 1$ and $r = 2i + 2$. If $\ell \ge |a|$, then $i$ has no smaller child. Otherwise the smaller child of $i$ is $r$ when $r < |a|$ and $a_r < a_\ell$, and $\ell$ in every other case, so ties go to the left child.

results.title: The smaller child has a larger index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $i < c$.

results.title: The smaller child is a valid index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $c$ is less than the length $|a|$ of $a$.

results.title: Sift-up
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and an index $i$, the sift-up of $a$ from $i$ is defined by recursion on $i$. If $i = 0$ or $i \ge |a|$, the result is $a$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$; if $a_i < a_p$, the result is the sift-up from $p$ of the array obtained from $a$ by exchanging the entries at positions $i$ and $p$, and…

results.title: Sift-down
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Sifting down an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type from index $i$ works as follows. If $i$ has a child in $a$, that is, if $2i+1$ is a valid index, let $c$ be the child of $i$ (among $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, if valid) holding the smaller value, preferring the left child $2i+1$ on ties. If $a_c < a_i$, swap the entries at $i$ and $c$ and continue sifting down from $c$; otherwise, or if $i$ has no child, return the…

results.title: Sift-up permutes the array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.

results.title: Binary-heap sift-down permutes the array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.

results.title: Binary-heap sift-up preserves the multiset of entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.

results.title: Binary-heap sift-down preserves the multiset of entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.

results.title: The root of a heap-ordered binary-heap array is minimal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered, then $a_0 \le a_i$ for every valid index $i$ of $a$.

results.title: Sift-up restores heap order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ be an index such that $a$ is ready for sift-up at $i$. Then the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is heap ordered.

results.title: Sift-down restores heap order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type that satisfies the sift-down precondition at a valid index $i$: the only edges that may violate heap order are those leaving $i$, and moving either child of $i$ up to position $i$ keeps the edge entering $i$ ordered. Then the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is heap-ordered.

results.title: Appending to a heap-ordered array prepares it for sift-up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered and $x$ is any value, then the array obtained by appending $x$ to $a$ satisfies the sift-up precondition at index $n$, the position of $x$: the only edge that may violate heap order is the one entering index $n$.

results.title: Binary min-heap
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ is an array $a$ of elements of $\alpha$ (its level-order storage), of length $|a|$ and with entries $a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, that is heap ordered: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the entry $a_{\lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor}$ at the parent index of $i$ is at most $a_i$.

results.title: Elements of a binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The multiset of elements of a binary min-heap is the multiset of the entries of its level-order storage array, counted with multiplicity.

results.title: Empty binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty binary min-heap is the min-heap whose level-order storage array has no entries.

results.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: To insert a value $x$ into a binary min-heap $h$, append $x$ at the end of the level-order array of $h$ and sift it up from its index (the old length of the array), repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it is smaller. The result is again a binary min-heap.

results.title: Minimum lookup in a binary heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$, the minimum lookup returns the entry at index $0$ (the root) of the storage array of $h$ when that array is nonempty, and returns no value when it is empty.

results.title: Binary heap minimum lookup fails exactly when empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns no value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has size $0$.

results.title: Binary heap minimum lookup succeeds exactly when nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns a value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has positive size.

results.title: The binary heap minimum lookup returns a stored element
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: The binary heap minimum lookup is a lower bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: Elements after binary heap insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$ added.

results.title: Binary heap insertion adds one copy of the inserted value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is one more than its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: Binary heap insertion leaves other multiplicities unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and let $x \ne y$ be values. Then $y$ occurs in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ exactly as many times as it occurs in the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap preserves heap order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the level-order array of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot index $i$ is at least the entry at its parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.

results.title: Moving the last entry to the root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ of length $n$, this operation swaps the entries at indices $0$ and $n - 1$ and then deletes the final entry. The result has length $n - 1$; when $n \ge 2$ its entry at index $0$ is $a_{n-1}$ and its entry at each index $0 < i < n - 1$ is $a_i$.

results.title: Moving the last entry to the root prepares a sift-down
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be a heap-ordered array over a linearly ordered type with at least two entries, and let $b$ be the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root. Then $b$ is ready for sifting down at index $0$: index $0$ is valid in $b$, and for every index $j > 0$ of $b$ whose parent index $\lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ is not $0$, the entry of $b$ at the parent index is at most $b_j$.

results.title: Moving the last entry to the root removes the old root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of entries of the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root equals the multiset of entries of $a$ with one occurrence of $a_0$ removed.

results.title: Removing the root of a nonempty binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type whose level-order array is nonempty. If the array has exactly one entry, the result is the empty heap. Otherwise the last entry of the array replaces the root, the array shrinks by one, and the result is the heap obtained by sifting this entry down from the root.

results.title: Extracting the minimum of a binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extraction returns nothing when the level-order array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it returns the root entry (the first entry of the array) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root and restoring heap order.

results.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap fails exactly when it is empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum of $h$ returns no result if and only if the level-order storage array of $h$ has size $0$.

results.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is one of its elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is minimal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x \le y$ for every value $y$ in the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: Elements after binary heap extraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by erasing one occurrence of $x$.

results.title: Binary heap extraction splits off the minimum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ equals the multiset of elements of $h'$ with one copy of $x$ added.

results.title: Binary heap extraction removes one copy of the minimum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of $h'$ is its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.

results.title: Binary heap extraction leaves other multiplicities unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then every value $y \ne x$ occurs in the multiset of elements of $h'$ exactly as many times as in the multiset of elements of $h$.

results.title: Membership after extraction from a binary min-heap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and suppose extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$. Then every value $y \ne x$ is an element of $r$ if and only if it is an element of $h$.

results.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap leaves a heap-ordered array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then the level-order array of $r$ is heap ordered: every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry.

results.title: The heap parent is one level up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $i > 0$, the parent index $p = \lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ satisfies $\lfloor \log_2(p+1) \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$; that is, in the level-order binary tree the parent of a nonroot index lies one level above it.

results.title: Sift-up with comparison and swap counts
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, this computes the sift-up of $a$ at $i$ together with a cost $(c, s) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $c$ counts value comparisons and $s$ counts swaps. If $i \ge |a|$ or $i = 0$, the result is $a$ with cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$. If $a_i < a_p$, the result is this sift-up…

results.title: Counting does not change the result of sift-up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the array returned by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ equals the array returned by the plain sift-up of $a$ at $i$.

results.title: Comparison bound for sift-up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.

results.title: Swap bound for sift-up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of swaps counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.

results.title: Combined comparison and swap bound for sift-up
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, if sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ counts $c$ comparisons and $s$ swaps, then $c + s \le 2 \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$.

results.title: Sift-up at the root costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $0$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

results.title: Sift-up at an out-of-range index costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$ with $i \ge |a|$, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

results.title: Decrease-key in a binary min-heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, an index $i < |a|$ and a value $x \le a_i$, decrease-key returns the heap whose array is obtained from $a$ by replacing the entry at position $i$ with $x$ and then sifting position $i$ up, repeatedly swapping the entry with its parent while it is strictly smaller than the parent.

results.title: Array of a binary heap after decrease-key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ equals the result of sifting up position $i$ in the array obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry at position $i$ with $x$.

results.title: Decrease-key yields a heap-ordered array
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot position is at least the entry at its parent position.

results.title: Decrease-key preserves the heap size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ has the same length as $a$.

results.title: Multiset of a binary heap after decrease-key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $a_i$ and adding one occurrence of $x$.

results.title: The smaller child lies one level below its parent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor = \lfloor \log_2 (i+1) \rfloor + 1$; that is, in the level-order binary tree stored in $a$, the node $c$ lies exactly one level below $i$.

results.title: The smaller child's level is bounded by the array size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor \le \lfloor \log_2 |a| \rfloor$.

results.title: Timed smaller-child selection
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, with left child $2i + 1$ and right child $2i + 2$; cost is counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). If both children are valid indices of $a$, the selection costs $(1, 0)$ and returns the right child when its value is strictly less than the value at the left child, and the left child otherwise. If only the left child is a valid index,…

results.title: Timed child selection returns the smaller child
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the value returned by timed child selection at $i$, with its cost discarded, is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$ (an optional index, absent when $i$ has no valid child).

results.title: Sift-down with comparison and swap counts
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, timed sift-down returns an array together with a cost pair (value comparisons, array swaps), where costs add componentwise. If the left child index $2i+1$ is not a valid index of $a$, it returns $a$ at cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $c$ be the smaller child of $i$: the left child $2i+1$, unless the right child $2i+2$ is a valid index and…

results.title: Timed sift-down returns the sift-down result
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array returned by timed sift-down from $i$, with its cost discarded, equals the array returned by sift-down from $i$.

results.title: Cost of child selection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, and count cost as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). The timed child selection at $i$ in $a$ has cost $(1, 0)$ if the right child index $2i + 2$ is less than the size of $a$, and cost $(0, 0)$ otherwise.

results.title: Child selection at a node without children costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then the timed child selection at $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$.

results.title: Sift-down performs at most one swap per remaining level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $\max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

results.title: Sift-down makes at most two comparisons per remaining level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $2 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

results.title: Total sift-down cost is at most three per remaining level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons plus the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $3 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

results.title: Sift-down from a node without children costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then sift-down from $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$: it makes no value comparisons and no array swaps.

results.title: Sift-down from a leaf costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be an index with $|a| \le 2i+1$, so that the left child of $i$ is not a valid index (this includes invalid indices $i$). Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

results.title: Sift-down from an invalid index costs nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be a natural number with $|a| \le i$. Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

path: Euler–Lotka equation and the reproduction number

results.title: Reproductive number from growth rate and generation interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The reproductive number implied by growth rate `r` and generation-interval law `g`: `R = 1 / M_g(-r)` (Wallinga–Lipsitch 2007, eq. 2.9).

results.title: Convex order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `g₁ ≤cx g₂` if `∫ φ dg₁ ≤ ∫ φ dg₂` for every convex `φ : ℝ → ℝ` that is integrable under both laws (Shaked–Shanthikumar 2007, §3.A).

results.title: Renewal equation for exponential growth
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `c ≠ 0`, the exponential `b(t) = c e^{r t}` solves `b(t) = R ∫ b(t - a) g(da)` for every `t` iff `R M_g(-r) = 1`. This is meaningful when `a ↦ e^{-r a}` is `g`-integrable; otherwise Lean's integral and `M_g(-r)` are both `0` and both sides of the equivalence are false.

results.title: Euler–Lotka
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under the hypotheses of `renewal_exp_iff`, exponential growth at rate `r` solves the renewal equation iff `R = 1 / M_g(-r)`.

results.title: Positivity of the reproductive number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The reproductive number is positive when `M_g(-r)` is finite.

results.title: Fixed generation interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Fixed generation interval `T`: `R = e^{r T}` (for all real `r`, `T`).

results.title: Gamma generation interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Gamma generation interval with shape `α > 0` and rate `β > 0`: for `r > -β`, `R = (1 + r / β)^α`.

results.title: Exponential generation interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Exponential generation interval with mean `T > 0` (rate `1 / T`): for `r T > -1`, `R = 1 + r T` (Wallinga–Lipsitch 2007, eq. 3.1).

results.title: More spread lowers `R`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `g₁ ≤cx g₂` and both have finite `M(-r)`, then `R(g₂) ≤ R(g₁)` at growth rate `r` (any real `r`). In particular, among generation intervals with a given mean, the fixed interval maximizes `R`.

results.title: Jensen bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the generation interval has finite mean `T̄ = ∫ a g(da)` and finite `M_g(-r)`, then `R ≤ e^{r T̄}` (any real `r`); Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007, §3) note that the fixed interval gives this upper bound.
